opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things I think the field has been a little sloppy about. People tend to lump everything a model gets wrong into one bucket and call it "out of distribution," but those failures come from very different places and you fix them in very different ways.

The way I like to think about it is to start from the data distribution itself rather than from the model's errors. A challenging in-domain example is something that comes from the same underlying generative process as your training data, just from a sparser or harder region of it. Think of a pedestrian partially occluded at dusk in a driving dataset. You've seen pedestrians, you've seen dusk, you've seen occlusion. That particular combination is rare and hard, but it lives inside the support of your distribution. A truly out-of-domain example comes from a different process. Maybe the camera sensor changed, maybe you trained on daytime suburban scenes and now you're deployed on a snowy rural road, or someone shows a classifier a category it was never meant to handle.

So how do you tell them apart in practice? A few things.

First, look at the representation, not just the output. If you embed your data with a reasonably strong model and look at where a failure case sits, hard in-domain examples tend to fall near the boundaries or tails of existing clusters. They have neighbors that look like them. Out-of-domain samples tend to sit in regions where there is essentially nothing nearby. Neighborhood density and distance to the nearest training samples tell you a lot.

Second, look at the kind of uncertainty. Hard in-domain examples usually produce confusion between plausible classes, the model is torn between "cyclist" and "pedestrian." Out-of-domain inputs often produce a different signature: the model can be confidently wrong, or the uncertainty is spread in ways that don't map onto any sensible confusion. Separating aleatoric uncertainty, ambiguity in the data itself, from epistemic uncertainty, the model just hasn't seen this, is a useful lens, even if the estimators are imperfect.

Third, and this is where I'd push people hardest, actually look at the data. A lot of what gets called a model problem is a data problem. When you do failure analysis by clustering errors and inspecting them, patterns pop out quickly. You'll find a slice of hard but legitimate cases you're underrepresenting, and separately a slice of images from a different camera or with corrupted labels or that simply shouldn't be in scope.

That distinction matters because the remedies differ. For hard in-domain cases, you go mine more of that tail, you annotate more carefully, maybe you rebalance or augment. For out-of-domain cases, more of the same data won't help. You need to decide whether to expand the domain deliberately, collecting new data and adapting, or to build a detector that recognizes "this isn't what I was built for" and defers or abstains.

I'd add one caveat: the line isn't perfectly crisp. Domain is a spectrum, and today's out-of-domain often becomes tomorrow's hard in-domain once you collect data for it. So I think of it less as a binary label and more as a question you keep asking about your system: where does this sample sit relative to what I've actually taught the model, and what's the right intervention given that?

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's actually one of the central questions we think about, and I'd say the honest answer is that the boundary is blurrier than people would like it to be. Let me unpack it a bit.

When you train a model, you've implicitly defined a distribution through your training data. A hard in-domain example is one that lives inside that distribution but sits in a region where the model has low density or high ambiguity. Think about a pedestrian detector that's seen tens of thousands of people standing upright, and now you show it someone crouching to tie their shoe, or partially occluded by a shopping cart. The concept is the same. The visual manifestation is just rare. The model should, in principle, be able to handle it with more data from that region, and often it fails gracefully. Confidence drops, the box jitters, but the failure mode makes sense.

A truly out-of-domain example is different in kind, not degree. It's a sensor modality the model never saw, a thermal image when you trained on RGB. It's a semantic category that doesn't exist in your label space. It's nighttime when all your training data was daytime, and that's not just a lighting shift, it changes what features are even present in the pixels. The telltale sign there is that the model fails confidently. It'll assign a high score to something absurd because the input lands in a region of feature space where it's extrapolating with no basis.

So the practical way we try to separate them is to stop reasoning about it from the model's output alone and instead look at the data itself. If you embed your training set and the new example, and the new example sits in a sparse but populated neighborhood, that's a hard in-domain case. If it's isolated, far from any support, you're probably out of domain. Density estimation in a good representation space is really the tool here, more than looking at softmax confidence, which we know is miscalibrated.

The other test I like is almost a human test. Could an annotator, given your labeling guidelines, label this example without the guidelines changing? If yes, it's in-domain and just hard. If the annotator says, "I don't know what to do with this," because the taxonomy doesn't cover it, that's your signal that you've left the domain.

And where this matters most is operationally. A hard in-domain example is a data problem. You go find more examples like it, you label them, you retrain. An out-of-domain example is a scope problem. You either expand the problem definition, or you build a mechanism that detects it and declines to answer. Treating one as the other is where a lot of deployed systems get into trouble.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is whether the example is difficult within the world your model is supposed to understand, or whether it comes from outside that world. An in-domain example might have an unusual viewpoint, heavy occlusion, or poor lighting. It’s challenging, but the objects and the task still fit the assumptions under which you trained the model.

An out-of-domain example breaks some of those assumptions. If you train on street scenes and then give the model a medical image, that’s a fairly clear case. But the boundary gets much less clear when you move from one city to another, or from daytime to nighttime. Whether that counts as out of domain depends on how you defined the domain in the first place.

So I wouldn’t distinguish them just by whether the model makes a mistake or has low confidence. A model can struggle with a perfectly valid in-domain example, and it can be very confident on something outside its domain. You need to look at the data and the intended operating conditions, not just the prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is whether the example is difficult within the world your model is supposed to understand, or whether it comes from a world that your model hasn’t learned. An image can be challenging because of occlusion, lighting, or an unusual viewpoint, while still being an in-domain example. If I’m detecting cars, a partially hidden car at night may be hard, but it’s still part of the task.

Out-of-domain means something has shifted beyond that expected operating environment. Maybe I trained on street-level photographs and now I’m looking at aerial imagery. There may still be cars, but the visual evidence is very different.

And the boundary isn’t always clean. You have to define what you mean by the domain and what variation you expect the system to handle. Low confidence alone doesn’t distinguish the two: a model can be uncertain on a hard in-domain example, and it can be confidently wrong on something completely outside its experience.
